chapters.title: Chapter 3: Signal Decay and Crowding: When an Edge Gets Discovered

lessons.title: Alpha Decay: Why Every Edge Has a Half-Life

children.text: Chapters 1 and 2 covered how size erodes returns: trade too much relative to liquidity and impact cost eats the edge. This chapter covers a second, separate threat that has nothing to do with how much capital you are running. An edge can shrink purely with the passage of time, as the market around it changes and other participants discover the same thing you did. That process is called alpha decay.
Alpha Decay vs Capacity: Two Different Threats

columns.label: Capacity Constraint
points: Caused by trading too much size relative to available liquidity
Can affect a strategy on day one if launched too large
A function of your own AUM versus liquidity, fixed at any point in time
Managed by trading smaller, spreading across a broader universe, or slower execution

columns.label: Alpha Decay
points: Caused by the underlying edge itself shrinking over time
Emerges gradually, sometimes over years, even for a trader running tiny size
A function of time and competitive discovery, independent of your own AUM
Cannot be solved by trading smaller, since the opportunity itself is what is shrinking

markDefs.definition: The tendency for a strategy's excess return over its benchmark or expected baseline to shrink over time, as the mispricing it exploits becomes more widely known or the conditions that created it change.

children.text: is the tendency for a strategy's excess return to fade over time. A signal that reliably generated 20 percent annualized alpha five years ago might generate a fraction of that today, not because it was ever wrong, but because the specific inefficiency it exploited has been partly closed by everyone else who eventually noticed it too.
Half-Life: Borrowing a Concept From Physics

A useful simplification, borrowed from radioactive decay, models alpha as fading exponentially over a characteristic half-life: the time it takes for excess return to fall to half of its starting value. This is a modeling convenience, not a precise physical law, but it broadly matches what academic research on published trading anomalies has found: return-predicting signals tend to weaken noticeably once they become public knowledge, whether through an academic paper, a widely read blog post, or simply enough desks converging on the same idea independently.

children.text: Why Edges Decay: Three Common Causes

cells: An academic paper, blog post, or well-attended talk describes the pattern, and desks systematically test and start trading it

More desks build similar systematic strategies as data, compute, and broker API access such as Zerodha's Kite Connect become cheaper and more widely available, without any single publication triggering it
The market condition that created the inefficiency changes, through regulation, exchange microstructure changes, or a shift in the macro regime, making the old edge irrelevant regardless of crowding

markDefs.definition: A standard measure of a signal's predictive power, typically the correlation between the signal's forecast (or rank) and the return that actually followed. A declining IC over time is one of the clearest quantitative signs of alpha decay.

children.text: Half-life is far easier to observe after the fact than to predict in advance, but there are leading indicators worth tracking. Compute the strategy's

, or IC, on a rolling basis and watch its trend rather than any single period's value. Watch whether the raw signal itself, before any trading, is shrinking in magnitude or dispersion across the universe. And watch whether your strategy's return stream is becoming more correlated with other systematic strategies you know about, an early symptom of the crowding covered in the next lesson.

body.title: Apply the Half-Life Formula
body.prompt: A strategy launches with 20% annualized alpha. Its estimated half-life is 3 years. Assuming pure exponential decay, what is its expected annualized alpha after 6 years, as a percentage?
body.explanation: 6 years is exactly 2 half-lives (6 / 3 = 2). Alpha = 20% x (1/2)^2 = 20% x 0.25 = 5%.

children.text: What Alpha Decay Does Not Mean

body.text: Decay is not a verdict that a strategy was wrong or that you made a mistake building it. It is the ordinary lifecycle of an edge in a competitive market. It is also not an excuse to panic-abandon a strategy after one weak year, since a genuine multi-year decay trend looks very different from ordinary noise around a still-intact edge. Telling the two apart, using a long enough sample and a rolling IC rather than a single bad quarter, is exactly the kind of judgment prop trading and quant research interviews probe for.
Capacity asks how much of an edge your own capital can absorb. Alpha decay asks how much of that edge is even still there. Both questions matter, and neither one answers the other.

points: Alpha decay is the tendency for a strategy's excess return to shrink over time, distinct from capacity, since it happens independently of how much capital you personally deploy.
Modeling decay as exponential, with a characteristic half-life, is a useful simplification broadly consistent with how published trading anomalies tend to behave once widely known.
Edges decay through public disclosure, independent convergence as more desks build similar strategies, and structural or regime change, not always through any one identifiable cause.
A declining rolling Information Coefficient is a more reliable early signal of genuine decay than a single bad period, which is often just noise around an edge that is still intact.
